entries.modern_form: PIE *gʷeyH- / *gʷyeh₁- 'to overpower, prevail, conquer' (Pokorny gʷeiə-, IEW 469-470; LIV *gʷyeh₁-)
entries.note: Pokorny p.469-470 has exactly this root: 'Root / lemma: gʷeiə-, Meaning: to prevail, be mighty', with Skt. jáyati 'overpowers, defeats', jyā́ 'force', Av. jayāi 'to defeat, conquer', Av. zinā-/zyā- 'damage', Gk. bía 'force'. Watkins (AHD appendix) has the same root as 'gʷeiə-. To press down, conquer. Sanskrit jayati, he conquers. [Pok. gʷeiə- 469]'. Nourai's twin citation form 'Gweie, Gweye' renders the two ablaut shapes gʷei-ə- / gʷeyə-; language label (Indo-European) and gloss ('to over power, defeat') are both right. The root as Pokorny states it is a bundle: the palatal-initial Iranian branch (zinā-, zyā- 'harm') and the labiovelar branch (Av. ǰay-, Skt. jayati, Gk. bía) are joined by him under one lemma, and modern handbooks (LIV) keep *gʷyeh₁- 'überwältigen' with the same members. The two doubtful members of Nourai's chart are the Avestan 'gā-' box (#3) and the Old English quench box (#8), see there.
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ بازسازی‌شدهٔ هندواروپایی آغازین *gʷeyH-/*gʷyeh₁- به معنی «چیره شدن، شکست دادن» است؛ پوکورنی (ایو ۴۶۹–۴۷۰) آن را با همین معنا آورده و سنسکریت jáyati «چیره می‌شود»، اوستایی ǰay- «پیروز شدن» و zyā-/zinā- «آسیب رساندن» و یونانی bía «زور» را ذیل آن نهاده است؛ واتکینز نیز در پیوست ریشه‌های هندواروپایی همان ریشه را با ارجاع به همان صفحهٔ پوکورنی آورده است. پس نام ریشه، برچسب زبانی و معنای آن در نمودار نورایی درست است. تنها دو شاخهٔ آن (اوستایی gā- «گاییدن» و انگلیسی کهن ācwencan) مورد تردید پژوهش امروزی است که در همان گره‌ها توضیح داده شده.

nodes.derivation: Bartholomae, AiWb col. 1707: 'j. zyā-; p. diyā- V. ‘schädigen’ (to damage). Praes. 11 zinā- ... Inf. zyānai', and cols. 1719 f. 'zyānay- f. ‘Schädigung’', 'zyānā- f. ‘Schädigung, Schaden’'. Nourai's 'zinât' is the 3sg. present zināṯ 'he injures' (nasal-infix present zi-nā- of the root zyā-), and 'zyâ 3, zyâni' are the root and the abstract noun zyāni- 'injury' (the 3 is the homonym number). Pokorny prints the same forms on p.469-470: 'Avestan zinat ‘damages’ ... Avestan zyana, zyani- f. ‘damage, harm’, Inf. zyanai ‘to harm’'; the palatal z- here goes back to the satem treatment of the initial, beside the labiovelar variant in Av. ǰay- (node #6) and Skt. jáyati, and Old Persian has the matching a-dinā-t 'he took away'.

nodes.derivation: Av. zyāni-/zyānā- 'damage' > Middle Persian zyān [zyʾn] 'loss, harm, damage' (MacKenzie, CPD 99) > New Persian ziyān, with the regular anaptyctic i breaking the initial cluster zy- (MP zyān is read ziyān already in Book Pahlavi practice). Parthian has the same word (Manichaean zyʾn), and the form was borrowed from Middle Iranian into Jewish Babylonian Aramaic zīyanā, Mandaic zāyinā, and Old Armenian zean; Kurdish and Pashto ziyān, Balochi ziyānī, Ossetic ziān are Persian loans (Horn no. 679). The meaning never shifted: 'harm, injury' > 'loss, damage'.
nodes.derivation_fa: «زیان» از فارسی میانهٔ zyān (نوشتهٔ zyʾn، در فرهنگ مکنزی: «loss, harm, damage») و آن از اوستایی zyāni-/zyānā- «آسیب» است؛ خوشهٔ آغازیِ zy- در فارسی نو با واکهٔ میانجی i شکسته شده و ziyān شده است. مؤلف در حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع (ص ۱۰۵۰ به بعد) همین را می‌گوید: «پهلوی zyān، اوستا zyāna-، zyāni- (ضرر)، بارتولمه ۱۷۰۷ و ۱۷۱۹؛ سانسکریت jyāni-». هرن (شمارهٔ ۶۷۹) نیز واژه‌های کردی، افغانی، بلوچی، آسی و ارمنی را وام از ایرانی می‌داند. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: The two words are real only in a qualified sense and the arrow from *gʷeyH- is not the modern view. (a) 'gâmô': Horn p.197 no. 883 quotes 'aw. gāmō.bərəti- ‘Coitus’ (nach Geiger, Ostiran. Kultur, 341 n.2)' — i.e. the sense rests on Geiger's interpretation of a compound; Bartholomae's AiWb has no Avestan gāmō 'coitus' at all (only gāya- 'step, pace' and its compounds, and mayah- 'Begattung' for 'coitus'). (b) The verb root 'gā 2 to rape' is likewise not an Avestan lemma in Bartholomae; it is the Iranian verb reconstructed from Middle and New Iranian. (c) The genealogy: Pokorny (469-470) mentions the family only as a hesitant aside — 'after Lidén IF. 19, 328 with npers. gāyad ‘futuit’, Inf. gādan, gān, from a root *gʷai- or (?) *gʷōi-, which would be compatible only with the latter beginning with gʷei- as lengthened grade of the o-gradation at most theoretically'. Cheung (Etym. Dict. of the Iranian Verb, s.v. *gaH² 'to have sexual intercourse') keeps the root separate and says 'The root *gaH is probably etymologically related to *gaH¹ [‘to go, stride’, PIE *gʷeh₂-]', a euphemism that 'has largely replaced the old IE root *Hiab'. So the modern account derives the word from 'to go/come (to)', not from 'to overpower'.
nodes.derivation_fa: این گره مورد اختلاف است. «gāmō» تنها بر پایهٔ خوانش گایگر از ترکیب اوستایی gāmō.bərəti- به معنی «آمیزش» است که هرن (ص ۱۹۷) نقل کرده؛ بارتولومه چنین واژه‌ای ندارد و در فرهنگ او تنها gāya- «گام» و mayah- «آمیزش» آمده است. ریشهٔ فعلی «gā» نیز مدخل اوستایی نیست بلکه بازسازی از ایرانی میانه و نو است. پوکورنی خودِ پیوند با ریشهٔ *gʷeyH- را تنها با تردید و به نقل از لیدن آورده و آن را «دست‌بالا از دید نظری ممکن» خوانده است، و چونگ در فرهنگ ریشه‌شناختی فعل‌های ایرانی این ریشه را *gaH² «آمیزش کردن» می‌داند و آن را به احتمال زیاد با *gaH¹ «رفتن» (هندواروپایی *gʷeh₂-) پیوند می‌زند، یعنی کاربردی حُسنِ تعبیری. پس پژوهش امروزی این پیکان را نمی‌پذیرد.

nodes.derivation: MP gādan/gāy- continues unbroken into New Persian: the old infinitive گادن gādan (now obsolete/dialectal) with past stem گاد gād and present stem گای gāy-, beside the secondary infinitive گاییدن gāyīdan built on the present stem — exactly the two script forms and the two stems Nourai prints. Horn p.197: 'gāden ‘coitiren’, Praes. gāy-em, gāyīden, gāye, gūn ‘Coitus’', with the Iranian cognates Kurd. gāyīn, Pashto γaγ/γōmə, Ossetic qāyun, Balochi gāy. Abolghasemi (FFD p.70) states the same: 'گاد < فارسی میانه gād؛ امروزه «گایید» به جای «گاد» به کار می‌رود ... گای < فارسی میانه gāy'. The only thing this node does not carry is a connection to the chart's root (see node #3).

nodes.derivation: These are the labiovelar branch of the root in Avestan, where Nourai's ž- stands for the palatal affricate ǰ of standard transcription. Bartholomae AiWb: 'j. ⁴ǰyā- V. ‘debilitare, minuere’. Praes. 11 ǰinā-, ... Inf. ǰyāi. — ǰināiti ‘debilitat’ F.35', with the note 'd. i. ǰiy-, daher auch ǰay° geschrieben' — so Nourai's 'žya 4' is literally Bartholomae's homonym-number 4 ǰyā-, and 'žayâi' is the infinitive ǰyāi in its ǰay- spelling. Pokorny p.469-470 gives both senses: 'Avestan ǰayāi, full grade of the root, ‘to defeat, conquer’' and 'Avestan ǰyā-, present ǰināiti ‘exhausts, weakens’'. Nourai's gloss 'defeated, diluted' is a loose English rendering of 'debilitare, minuere' ('weakened, diminished') — 'diluted' is infelicitous but not wrong in intent.

nodes.derivation: The Old English word is real: ācwencan 'to quench, extinguish (fire, light)', the causative of cwincan 'to go out, be extinguished, vanish'. What is disputed is the arrow from the IE root. Pokorny does draw it — under gʷeiə- he lists 'Middle High German verquīnen ... Old English cwīnan, a-cwīnan ‘dwindle away’, extended Old English cwincan, acwincan ‘disappear’ (Kaus. with ablaut neologism acwencan, engl. quench)' — but modern Germanic etymology does not: Etymonline, s.v. quench, gives 'Old English acwencan ‘to quench’, from Proto-Germanic *kwenkjanan, probably a causative from the source of Old English cwincan ... No certain cognates outside Germanic; perhaps a substratum word', and Watkins' AHD appendix (which Nourai cites) has no QUENCH under gʷeiə- or any other root. So the word belongs to a Germanic family of unclear ultimate origin, and the IE derivation drawn here is Pokorny's 1959 guess only.

nodes.derivation: Greek βάλλω 'I throw, cast, hurl' (aor. ἔβαλον, perf. βέβληκα), from *gʷl̥-n-h₁- with the nasal infix, is the central IE reflex of the root. The compounds are all classical and glossed correctly: παραβάλλω 'to throw beside, set side by side, compare' (whence παραβολή 'comparison, parable' — the source of parler/parable, node #4); συμβάλλω 'to throw together, compare' (whence σύμβολον, the token whose two halves are matched); διαβάλλω 'to throw across; to set at variance, slander', whence the agent noun διάβολος 'slanderer', which in the Septuagint and New Testament renders Hebrew śāṭān and so becomes 'the Devil'. The prefix cross-references Nourai gives (Per 1 = περί/παρά, Sem 1 = σύν, Dwo = διά, from *dwo- 'two') are the standard analyses.

nodes.derivation: All seven are Greek words that reached English through Latin (some through French): ballistic (1775, from Latin ballista), parabola (1570s, Latin parabola < παραβολή), hyperbola (1660s, ὑπερβολή 'a throwing beyond, excess'), metabolism (1878, μεταβολή 'change, a throwing about'), problem (late 14c., πρόβλημα 'a thing thrown forward, question put'), symbol (1590s, σύμβολον), devil (Old English dēofol, from Ecclesiastical Latin diabolus < διάβολος). Klein's ballistic entry lists precisely this set — 'amphibole, ... catabolism, devil, diabolic, ... hyperbola, hyperbole, metabolism, parable, parabola, ... problem, symbol' — so the box is exactly right; the only tacit shortcut is that devil entered Old English directly from Ecclesiastical Latin, several centuries before the learned Greek borrowings.
nodes.derivation_fa: هر هفت واژه یونانی‌اند که از راه لاتینی (و گاه فرانسوی) به انگلیسی رسیده‌اند: ballistic (۱۷۷۵، از لاتینی ballista)، parabola (۱۵۷۰م، از παραβολή)، hyperbola (۱۶۶۰م، از ὑπερβολή «فراافکنی، زیاده‌روی»)، metabolism (۱۸۷۸، از μεταβολή «دگرگونی»)، problem (اواخر سدهٔ چهاردهم، از πρόβλημα «آنچه پیش افکنده شود»)، symbol (۱۵۹۰م، از σύμβολον) و devil (انگلیسی کهن dēofol از لاتینی کلیسایی diabolus). کلاین در مدخل ballistic دقیقاً همین مجموعه را برمی‌شمارد. تنها نکتهٔ ناگفته آن است که devil چند سده پیش از وام‌واژه‌های عالمانه و مستقیماً از لاتینی کلیسایی وارد انگلیسی کهن شده است. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Arabic إبليس Iblīs, the Qurʾānic name of the Devil, is a loan from Greek διάβολος. Jeffery, Foreign Vocabulary of the Qurʾān p.47: 'Iblīs. διάβολος the Devil par excellence ... That the word is a corruption of the Gk. διάβολος has been recognized by the majority of Western scholars'; he notes that the Muslim philologers' derivation from أبلس ablasa 'to despair' was already rejected by al-Jawālīqī. Klein (Eblis, p.496-497) adds the transmission detail: 'Arab. Iblīs, aphetic for Gk. διάβολος ... It is very probable that Gk. διάβολος came into Arabic through the medium of Syriac and that the first syllable of the Greek word was mistaken for the Syriac genitive particle di and subsequently dropped'. The alternative Arabic-root etymology survives as a minority view (noted on Wiktionary), but the form ʾiF'īl is, as Jeffery says, otherwise reserved for foreign words.
nodes.derivation_fa: «ابلیس» در عربی وام‌واژه‌ای از یونانی διάβολος است. جفری در «واژگان دخیل در قرآن» ص ۴۷ می‌نویسد که «ابلیس تحریفِ διάβολος یونانی است و بیشتر خاورشناسان آن را پذیرفته‌اند» و می‌افزاید که اشتقاق آن از «أبلس یُبلس» (نومید شدن) را جوالیقی هم رد کرده است. کلاین (ص ۴۹۶–۴۹۷) می‌افزاید که این واژه احتمالاً از راه سریانی به عربی رسیده و هجای نخستِ آن (di) به اشتباه حرف اضافهٔ اضافیِ سریانی پنداشته و افتاده است. اشتقاقِ عربیِ آن امروز دیدگاهی اقلیتی است، چون وزن «إفعیل» جز در واژه‌های دخیل به‌کار نمی‌رود. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Greek βαλλίζω 'to dance, jump about' is a derivative of βάλλω, literally 'to throw one's body about' (ancient Greek dancing being highly athletic); it is attested chiefly in Sicilian and South-Italian Greek, which is exactly why it survived into Latin. Watkins puts it under the same root: 'b. Greek ballizein, to dance: BALL², (BALLAD), (BALLET), BAYADERE'; Klein: 'VL. ballare, fr. Gk. βαλλίζειν, ‘to dance’, which prob. derives fr. βάλλειν, ‘to throw’'.

nodes.derivation: Correct in substance, compressed in route. French bal 'a dance, dancing party' is the verbal noun of Old French baller 'to dance' (12c.), from Late Latin ballāre, itself the borrowing of Greek βαλλίζειν — so bal is two steps, not one, from the Greek. French ballet is later and comes back through Italy: 1660s, from Italian balletto, diminutive of ballo 'a dance' (from ballāre), taken into French with the court spectacle of the 16th-17th c. Neither word is a direct French continuation of a Greek verb, which is what the single arrow suggests.

nodes.derivation: Persian بالت bālet is a 20th-century French loan (ballet), taken with the European performing arts along with اپرا, تئاتر, ارکستر; the Persian spelling بالت reproduces the French pronunciation [balɛ] with the final -t of the French orthography, whence the older Persian rendering bālet, while the now-usual form is باله bāle, closer to the spoken French. No Arabic or Turkish mediation is involved.

nodes.derivation: Both belong to this family but neither comes straight from Greek. ballroom is an English compound (1690s) of ball 'dancing party' + room, and ball (n.2) is a 1630s borrowing of French bal (< Old French baller < Late Latin ballāre < βαλλίζειν). ballad is Middle English balade, from Old French balade, from Old Provençal balada 'a dance; a song to dance to', from balar 'to dance', again from Late Latin ballāre. So the Greek > English arrow skips Late Latin plus a Romance stage in each case; the etymology itself is uncontested.
